nodes.title: create_geowc
nodes.summary: Create a geostrophic wind climate dataset.
nodes.doc:
Create a geostrophic wind climate dataset.

A geostrophic wind climate is a binned wind climate of the *geostrophic* wind, so this is :func:`create_bwc` with three differences: * the wind is stronger, so the Weibull scale and the wind speed axis both reach further - the default axis runs to 60 m s-1 and the distribution peaks near 14, against 30 and 5 for a surface climate; * the speed and direction frequencies are combined into a single ``geo_wv_freq``, which sums to 1 over the whole ``(wsbin, sector)`` array rather than to 1 within each sector; and * the mesoscale roughness description and the geostrophic turning are added. Everything else - sampling the Weibull at the bin centres, and keeping the distribution inside the wind speed axis instead of cutting it off on its own slope - comes from :func:`create_bwc`, so those rules are defined once.

inputs.doc: Output geospatial information.

fields.name: n_sectors

fields.name: n_wsbins
fields.doc: Number of wind speed bins, defaults to 60. Geostrophic winds are much stronger than surface winds, so the axis has to reach far higher than for a binned wind climate.

fields.name: wsbin_width
fields.doc: Width of each wind speed bin [m s-1], defaults to 1.0.

fields.name: not_empty

fields.name: seed

fields.typeText: float, tuple of float, or None

nodes.title: create_gewc
nodes.summary: Create a synthetic generalized extreme wind climate.
nodes.doc:
Create a synthetic generalized extreme wind climate.

"Generalized" means 10 m above a homogeneous surface of roughness 0.05 m - the condition LINCOM downscales from, and ``pywasp.lincom.v50_lut``'s ``DEFAULT_HGT`` and ``DEFAULT_Z0``. The annual maxima are drawn per point and sector from a Gumbel distribution, with the location and scale reduced away from the prevailing direction so that the wind rose is not flat. Directions fall inside their own sector bin. Because the generalized condition is fixed at 10 m, points at the same horizontal location receive the same climate at every height. The repetition is deliberate and permitted by the ``"optional"`` height policy of the maxima: LINCOM consumes a generalized climate on the three-dimensional structure of its output points.

fields.name: location_range

fields.name: scale_range
fields.doc: Bounds of the per-point Gumbel scale parameter [m s-1]. Defaults to ``(1.2, 2.5)``.

fields.name: prevailing_direction
fields.doc: Direction of the strongest sector [degrees]. Defaults to 270.

fields.name: directional_contrast

nodes.title: create_surface_fields
nodes.summary: Create synthetic mesoscale surface fields as a time series.
nodes.doc:
Create synthetic mesoscale surface fields as a time series.

Produces the raw model output variables from which the surface-layer temperature scale is derived, using the WRF naming convention, alongside the wind time series from :func:`create_tswc`. Time-varying variables: ``PSFC``, ``T2``, ``UST``, ``HFX``, ``LH``, ``PBLH``, ``Q2``, ``ZNT``, ``wind_speed``, ``wind_direction``. Time-constant variables: ``LANDMASK``, ``elevation``. The stability variables these fields feed, ``temp_scale`` and ``ustar_over_pblh``, are not part of the mesoscale set. They can be added with the ``fields`` argument, which is resolved exactly as :func:`create_tswc` resolves its own; asking for them here generates them together with the surface fields, in one correlated draw, so that a point holds the reference correlations between the two groups as well - the ``temp_scale``/``HFX`` pair among them. Every point is over land: the values are drawn from an onshore reference, so ``LANDMASK`` is 1 everywhere and the fields carry no offshore behaviour. Code that has to exercise a land/sea contrast should set ``LANDMASK`` and the surface fields of the sea points itself. These are all surface variables: every one of them declares ``height_dim_policy: "forbidden"``, so none carries a height dimension in the returned dataset, whatever the structure of ``output_locs``. Each is drawn once per ``(west_east, south_north)`` column, so no two columns hold the same values — a fixture that repeated them could not detect code which loses track of which location a value belongs to. A column is identified by exact equality of its two coordinates, which holds for every structure windkit builds. ``wind_speed`` and ``wind_direction`` come from :func:`create_tswc` and keep their height dimension. Within a point the fields carry the cross-correlations of the reference site, including with ``wind_speed``.

inputs.name: output_locs
inputs.doc: Output geospatial information.

fields.name: date_range
fields.doc: Time range. If None, one month of 2001 at hourly resolution is used, which is small enough to stay a cheap fixture. It must span more than two days, whatever its resolution.

fields.name: not_empty
fields.doc: If True, the surface fields are filled with synthetic data. If False, every variable is NaN, as :func:`create_tswc` does. Defaults to True.

fields.name: seed
fields.doc: Seed for the random data, defaults to 9876538.

fields.name: ranges
fields.doc: Overrides for the ``(low, high)`` bounds of individual surface fields. Keys not given fall back to the module defaults, and keys outside the surface fields are rejected - the stability variables are bounded by ``fields`` instead. Each entry must have ``low < high``; neither the ordering nor the width of a pair is checked, so a reversed pair flips the field about its mid-range and an equal pair makes it constant.

fields.name: elevation_range
fields.doc: Bounds of the terrain elevation [m], with ``low < high``. Defaults to ``(0.0, 200.0)``.

fields.name: fields
fields.doc: Stability variables to generate alongside the surface fields, as in :func:`create_tswc`: ``None`` for none of them, ``"stability"`` or ``"all"`` for every one, or the names to generate. Unlike passing them to :func:`create_tswc` separately, these are drawn together with the surface fields, so the two groups are correlated with each other.
fields.typeText: str, sequence of str or None

nodes.ret: Time series of mesoscale surface fields.

nodes.title: create_tswc
nodes.summary: Create time series wind climate dataset.
nodes.doc:
Create time series wind climate dataset.

When ``not_empty=True`` (default), the data variables are filled with temporally and spatially correlated synthetic wind data using an AR(1) process in Gaussian space transformed to a Weibull distribution for speed, and a circular AR(1) with von Mises innovations for direction.

inputs.name: output_locs
inputs.doc: Output geospatial information.

fields.name: date_range
fields.doc: Time range as a pandas DateTimeIndex. If None is passed, a default range of one year (2001) at 10 min resolution is created.

fields.name: not_empty
fields.doc: If True, the empty dataset is filled with realistic synthetic wind data. Defaults to True.

fields.name: seed
fields.doc: Seed for the random data, defaults to 9876538.

fields.name: weibull_A
fields.doc: Weibull scale parameter [m/s]. Defaults to 8.0.

fields.name: weibull_k
fields.doc: Weibull shape parameter. Defaults to 2.1.

fields.name: speed_tau
fields.doc: Autocorrelation e-folding timescale for speed [s]. Defaults to 14400 (4 h).

fields.name: direction_mean
fields.doc: Prevailing wind direction [degrees]. Defaults to 240.

fields.name: direction_kappa
fields.doc: Von Mises concentration around prevailing direction. Defaults to 1.5.

fields.name: direction_tau
fields.doc: Autocorrelation timescale for direction [s]. Defaults to 21600 (6 h).

fields.name: spatial_correlation_length
fields.doc: Spatial e-folding length scale for inter-point correlation [same unit as coordinates]. Defaults to 10000.

fields.name: fields
fields.doc: Stability variables to add alongside the wind: ``"stability"`` or ``"all"`` for both ``temp_scale`` (:math:`T_*`) and ``ustar_over_pblh`` (:math:`u_*/z_i`), or a subset of those names. Defaults to None, which adds neither. The values are bounded by the 0.1st to 99.9th percentile of an onshore mesoscale reference and carry that reference's correlations with each other and with the generated wind speed. Both are surface-layer scales, declared ``height_dim_policy: "forbidden"``, so they are drawn once per horizontal column - driven by the wind at its lowest height - and carry no height dimension, while the wind keeps its own. ``temp_scale`` follows the convention in which :math:`T_*` has the sign of the surface heat flux, so positive is unstable and negative stable (https://doi.org/10.1007/s10546-023-00803-3).
fields.typeText: str, sequence of str or None

nodes.ret: Time series wind climate dataset.

nodes.title: create_v50_lut
nodes.summary: Create a synthetic LINCOM extreme wind lookup table.
nodes.doc:
Create a synthetic LINCOM extreme wind lookup table.

A lookup table answers "if the generalized wind is this fast, from this sector, what is the local wind here?". This builds one directly from a per-point, per-sector speedup and direction veer rather than by running LINCOM over terrain, so it is fast and every entry is distinct. The speedup does not depend on the generalized speed, which is what a linearised flow model gives; the local speed is therefore proportional to the generalized one at each anchor.

inputs.doc: Output geospatial information.

fields.name: gen_wspd

fields.name: n_sectors

fields.name: seed
fields.doc: Seed for the random data, defaults to 9876538.

fields.name: speedup_range

fields.name: veer_range
fields.doc: Bounds of the per-point, per-sector direction change [degrees]. Defaults to ``(-8.0, 8.0)``.

The key is a float with the height, and the value is a tuple (str,str) with the header for the wind speed and the header for the wind direction, respectively. nodes.title: rotor_equivalent_wind_speed
nodes.summary: Calculate the rotor equivalent wind speed (REWS) from given wind speed and directions on height levels.
nodes.doc:
Calculate the rotor equivalent wind speed (REWS) from given wind speed and directions on height levels.

The procedure is as follows: 1. Find the area of each segment of the rotor spanned area. 2. Calculate the wind speed at the center of each segment by linearly interpolating the wind speed to the height of the segment center in log-height. 3. Calculate the wind direction at the center of each segment by linearly interpolating the wind direction to the height of the segment center. Circularity is taken into account here. 4. Calculate the wind direction at hub height by linearly interpolating the wind direction to the hub height. 5. Calculate the REWS as the cube root of the sum of the wind speed at each segment center multiplied by the area-weight (area/total) of the segment and the cosine of the difference between the wind direction at the segment center and the wind direction at hub height.

nodes.title: plot.wind_rose
nodes.summary: Create wind rose plot.
nodes.doc:
Create wind rose plot.

The wind rose can be plotted in two different styles: - Simple wind rose which shows information regarding the wind direction for each sector. - Stacked wind rose which includes information for both the wind direction and the wind speed for each sector. The type of wind rose is controlled by the ``wind_speed_bins`` input which will define the style of the wind rose and, if it is desired, the wind speed intervals shown in the wind rose. Moreover, by using the style argument, one can define the plotting style of the wind rose: radar (line polar plot) or rose.

inputs.name: ds
inputs.doc: WindKit Dataset representing a either a binned "histogram" wind climate or a weibull wind climate in a single point.

fields.name: wind_speed_bins
fields.doc: Can take the following values: - None: results in a simple rose representation, representing only the wind direction frequency. (Default) - List of floats: Manually introduced list where each float defines one limit of each wind speed interval. e.g: wind_speed_bins = [0, 5.5, 10, 30] would create 3 gorups of wind speeds: 0 - 5.5, 5.5 - 10 and 10 - 30. Results in a stacked wind rose. - One of three different str ("IEC_I", "IEC_II" or "IEC_III"): Each class has predefined wind speed intervals that correspond to the turbine characteristics, defined in the plot.wind_rose module. Results in a stacked wind rose.

fields.name: style
fields.doc: Can take the following values: - "rose": the plotting style is a rose. - "radar": the plotting style is a line polar plot. By default is defined as "rose".

fields.name: uniform_color
fields.doc: Determines the uniform color when representing the simple rose. Strings should define valid CSS-colors. By default is defined as "blue".

fields.name: cmap
fields.doc: Determines the sequential color scale when representing the stacked wind rose. Strings should define valid built-in sequential color scales' names. By default is defined as "Viridis_r".

fields.name: gap
fields.doc: Include a gap between sectors? (Default: no gap)

nodes.ret: Plotly figure for display, additional modification, or output

nodes.doc:
Download ERA5 data from the planetary computer.

Read about Microsofts planetary computer here: https://planetarycomputer.microsoft.com/docs/overview/about Use of Microsofts Planetary Computer is subject to Planetary Computer terms of service: https://planetarycomputer.microsoft.com/terms This function requires the optional dependencies: "zarr", "pystac-client", "planetary-computer", "fsspec", and "adlfs"

inputs.name: bbox
inputs.doc: Bounding box of the ERA5 data to download. Must be in "EPSG:4326" coordinates. If a list, tuple, or np.ndarray is provided, it must be a a 1D iterable of [min_lon, min_lat, max_lon, max_lat]. By default None, which downloads the entire ERA5 grid.

fields.name: datetime
fields.doc: Either a single datetime or datetime range used to filter results. If a tuple, it must be a (start, end) tuple of datetime.datetime or timestamps as described below. You may express a single datetime using a datetime.datetime instance, a RFC 3339-compliant timestamp, or a simple date string (see below). Instances of datetime.datetime are assumed to be in UTC timezone If using a simple date string, the datetime can be specified in YYYY-mm-dd format, optionally truncating to YYYY-mm or just YYYY. Simple date strings will be expanded to include the entire time period, If used in a range, the end of the range expands to the end of that day/month/year.

fields.name: source
fields.doc: Source from which we download the ERA5 data, by default "planetary_computer" Currently only "planetary_computer" is supported

fields.name: translate_to_windkit
fields.doc: If True, translate the ERA5 data to the format used in windkit, by default True

nodes.title: get_tutorial_data
nodes.summary: Download and extract tutorial data, returning the path to the folder.

Download and extract tutorial data, returning the path to the folder.

Downloads tutorial data from Zenodo if not already cached, extracts it, and returns the path to the extracted folder. Use ``load_tutorial_data`` to load the files into memory as windkit objects. The local cache is stored in the user data directory under the name "windkit". On Windows, this is typically located at: ``C:\Users\<username>\AppData\Roaming\windkit\tutorial_data`` On Linux, it is typically located at: ``/home/<username>/.local/share/windkit/tutorial_data`` You can check the location of the user data directory using the ``user_data_dir`` function from the ``platformdirs`` package.
